extracted.intended_audience: researchers and philosophers of mathematics, journal editors, and scholars of peer review and inter-rater agreement
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and critical analysis for using inter-rater agreement statistics (especially Cohen's κ) to assess mathematical peer review, including a toy model with parameters for error rate, reviewer mastery, positivity, and cohesion. Useful for researchers modeling peer review processes and for editors interpreting agreement data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohen's κ — definition and basic interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohen’s κ is a statistical measure for inter-rater agreement: κ = (F − E)/(1 − E), where F is the observed frequency of agreement and E is the expected (chance) agreement. κ = 1 corresponds to full agreement and κ = 0 corresponds to agreement equal to chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a standard measure of inter-rater agreement (Cohen 1960). It compares observed agreement to expected agreement under random distribution. Interpreters should be aware that the meaning of particular κ values is context-sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of κ as a proxy for sensitivity (when repeated independent tests available)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohen’s κ can be used as an informative proxy for the sensitivity of a checking mechanism when each sample is tested twice by independent tests and property prevalence is low: in such situations κ is close to the test sensitivity (probability of detecting property P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relies on independence of the tests and random distribution of the target property P; Table 1 in the paper illustrates that if prevalence ≤ 20%, κ approximates sensitivity well. This is applicable when the test is the only epistemic access to the property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kappa interpretation pitfalls and 'kappa paradoxes'
rubrics_metrics.description: The statistical literature documents undesirable behaviour of κ (the 'kappa paradoxes'): e.g., small κ despite high agreement when prevalence of the target property is very small, and other context-dependent anomalies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the Feinstein & Cicchetti paradoxes. Do not take numerical κ descriptors at face value; instead interpret κ in light of prevalence, specificity, and domain context. The paper references Feinstein & Cicchetti (1990) and related work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landis and Koch descriptors are arbitrary and context-sensitive
rubrics_metrics.description: The conventional numerical descriptors for κ ranges (Landis & Koch 1977) are arbitrary conventions and may not translate across application contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., what counts as 'substantial agreement' in a manufacturing quality check may be unacceptable for a medical diagnostic test. The paper cautions against uncritical use of these benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of prevalence and specificity (s) effects on κ
rubrics_metrics.description: κ depends on prevalence of the target property and the specificity of the test; high specificity combined with very low prevalence can produce paradoxically low κ values despite high agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including a specificity parameter s in the model substantially changes κ (see modified formulas and Table 2). Feuerman & Miller (2005, 2008) are cited for relationships between κ, sensitivity and specificity. Do not ignore specificity when interpreting κ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore alternative agreement measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Several alternatives to Cohen’s κ exist (Scott’s π, Holley & Guilford’s G-index, Bangdiwala’s B, Gwet’s AC1) which aim to ameliorate some unwanted features of κ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes many alternatives share the same mathematical structure and expects the toy-model conclusions would not differ substantially if another measure were used, but practitioners should consider alternatives especially when κ exhibits paradoxical behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toy-model parameter: Correctness (e, error probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions are either correct or incorrect; e (error probability) is the probability that a submission is fundamentally flawed (must not be published).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model simplifies reality by treating correctness as binary and ignoring partially correct / fixable errors. The paper uses example values e ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3} as realistic ranges based on editorial experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toy-model parameter: Mastery (m, reviewer sensitivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: m (mastery) is the probability that a referee detects a fundamental flaw (masterful = detects flaws). In biomedical terminology, mastery corresponds to sensitivity of the referee's flaw-testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The philosophical claim that mathematics is an 'epistemic exception' corresponds to the special case m = 1. The model shows κ may fail to detect m = 1 under realistic conditions. Mastery is confounded with reviewer effort (see resource-boundedness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Toy-model parameter: Positivity (p, subjective acceptance tendency)
rubrics_metrics.description: p (positivity) is the probability a referee recommends acceptance provided they have not detected a fundamental flaw — i.e., the subjective component of the decision (scope, novelty, taste).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positivity aggregates many subjective/non-correctness factors into one probability. The paper finds that κ is a poor proxy for m when p ≠ 1; realistic values of p (e.g., p ≤ 0.5) substantially reduce κ even when m = 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohesion parameter (c) — modelling social/community agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohesion c (≥ p^2 + (1 − p)^2) replaces the independent-chance agreement on non-flawed papers to model the tendency of a disciplinary community to agree more than chance on novelty/relevance judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher cohesion raises κ values and can minimise the effect of m on κ, making detection of epistemic exceptionality even harder. The paper presents Table 5 showing κ increases quickly with c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model assumptions and simplifications to note
rubrics_metrics.description: The toy model assumes binary correctness, no false positives (specificity = 1 in the simpler version), independence where assumed, and that subjective judgment is captured by p; it ignores partial corrections, false alarms later rectified, and many real-world subtleties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These simplifications are deliberate and (authors argue) only make it easier to detect epistemic exceptionality; still, users must be aware that relaxing assumptions (e.g., allowing false positives) alters formulas and κ behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource-boundedness confound (effort vs. epistemic ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if referees are in principle masterful (m = 1), they may not invest the time and energy to exercise that ability; κ cannot distinguish between perfect ability exercised only some fraction of the time and genuinely lower mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a structural problem: values of κ conflate true epistemic access with the fraction of referees who actually use it. Surveys (e.g., Geist et al. 2010) show many referees do not check proofs line-by-line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical inference limitation: κ cannot establish epistemic exceptionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Given realistic parameter ranges for e and p, κ values do not allow one to conclude that a reviewing system is in the epistemically exceptional case (m = 1); κ values for m = 1 can be indistinguishable from κ values for m < 1 under plausible e,p combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper gives numerical examples where worlds with m = 1 produce identical κ to worlds with m < 1. Thus κ-based empirical arguments for/against mathematics being epistemically exceptional are unsuccessful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for empirical parameter estimation and comparative studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Robust empirical estimates of parameters e (error prevalence), p (positivity), cohesion, and reviewer behaviour are lacking; the paper urges quantitative/ comparative empirical study to ground inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recommendations include measuring rejection reasons to estimate p for a journal, and comparative studies across disciplines to investigate cohesion effects that may explain higher κ in mathematics.
